sentence_given: I think you should complain about that horrible meal.
incomplete_phrase: If I ... a complaint about that horrible meal.

sentence_given: Christina had never visited Venice before.
incomplete_phrase: It was ... to Venice.

sentence_given: No matter how hard he tried, Victor couldn't open the box.
incomplete_phrase: Even ... , Victor couldn't open the box.

sentence_given: It isn't really worth trying to fly the kite when there's no wind.
incomplete_phrase: It ... fly the kite when there's no wind.

sentence_given: Oliver says he will only play football if he can be team captain.
incomplete_phrase: Oliver says that he ... he can be team captain.

sentence_given: Dancing was an activity that David had never wanted to do.
incomplete_phrase: Dancing was an activity that ... David.

sentence_given: Timothy doesn't understand how to do this task.
incomplete_phrase: Timothy ... to do this task.
explanation: A simple paraphrase is needed here. If you have no clue how to do something, it means you have no idea about it or how it works.

sentence_given: I will come to the party, I promise!
incomplete_phrase: He said that ... the party.
explanation: An example of reported speech with all the necessary transformations. Note that in different cases of reported speech you will need to change tense, prepositions and modal verbs.

sentence_given: Having run for ten minutes straight, I had difficulties breathing.
incomplete_phrase: I was ... I had been running for ten minutes straight.
explanation: To be out of breath means to have difficulty breathing because of physical exertion. Be aware of the differences in spelling: the verb is "to breathe", whereas the noun is "breath".

sentence_given: Working is much less tiring than simply doing nothing.
incomplete_phrase: Simply doing nothing is ... working.
explanation: 'Way more tiring' is an answer that would get you 1 point instead of 2 in the exam. That is because you are discouraged from introducing any additional changes unless they are necessary. 'Way' is more informal than 'much', even though it has the same meaning.

sentence_given: I don't think it is going to rain today.
incomplete_phrase: I think ... today.
explanation: The word 'fall' is optional here as it does not add anything to the sentence, however its addition does not change the meaning in a negative way either. Keep in mind that any transformation in FCE Use of English 4 has to be justified.

sentence_given: I missed the meeting because my car broke down.
incomplete_phrase: Had my car ... not have missed the meeting.
explanation: A case of Third Conditional sentence is present here - an unreal result of an action, that didn't take place. The usual structure is If + Past Perfect in the condition part and Present Perfect in the result part. Remember that with the conditionals you never use "if" and "will/would" in the same part of the sentence.

sentence_given: Our manager told me that quitting is not a good idea.
incomplete_phrase: I was ... our manager.
explanation: An important thing to keep in mind is the verb pattern - to discourage somebody from doing something. Only the gerund should be used after this particular structure. Knowing verb patterns helps with this part of the exam considerably.

sentence_given: The police are interrogating the suspect now.
incomplete_phrase: The suspect ... the police now.
explanation: A past continuous passive structure is required to make the transformation. Failing to use the continuous form will mean that you only get 1 out of the two points possible for this task.

sentence_given: This weather is very fitting for a picnic.
incomplete_phrase: This ... for a picnic.
explanation: An important note to make is that 'weather' is uncountable and doesn't require an article, even despite taking an adjective 'fitting' here. This is a trap as most students are used to the structure 'such a …' and are tempted to use it without thinking about the purpose of the indefinite article.

sentence_given: Dereck managed to avoid going to prison for the crime.
incomplete_phrase: Dereck ... the crime.
explanation: If you get away with something, you go unpunished for it. Here, the test-taker gets some leeway with the choice of words, the last part can be omitted altogether without affecting the meaning of the sentence.

sentence_given: They are blaming me for their own mistakes.
incomplete_phrase: They are ... their own mistakes.
explanation: To hold somebody accountable for something is to make them responsible for it. It is chiefly used in the negative meaning, e.g. somebody making a mistake and having to answer for it. 'To make somebody accountable' is not a collocation and should not be given as the answer.

sentence_given: Waking up early hardly improved her productivity.
incomplete_phrase: Waking up early ... to her productivity.
explanation: 'Hardly improved' in this context means that the improvement wasn't very big or noticeable. Therefore, we need to use 'much' achieve the same effect. Omitting the word 'good' changes the meaning considerably - it means that almost no effect was made, neither positive nor negative.

sentence_given: They are not in the mood for swimming right now.
incomplete_phrase: They ... right now.
explanation: To feel reluctant or unwilling to do something. Note the gerund form in this phrase.

sentence_given: My uncle holds that I should not agree to this deal.
incomplete_phrase: I should ... deal, according to my uncle.
explanation: A more informal phrasal verbs, 'to pull out of something' is used figuratively to mean to stop being a part of something like a business deal or a project.

sentence_given: I believe that you should continue studying at university.
incomplete_phrase: To ... stop studying at university.
explanation: The phrase 'to my mind' is a common way to paraphrase 'in my opinion', 'I think' or 'I believe'. An important point - you can use both 'should not' and 'shouldn't', however both would count as two words. In your exam paper, I would advise using the full form.

sentence_given: The trip was much better than they had expected.
incomplete_phrase: The trip ... as they had expected.
explanation: A comparative structure 'as … as ...' is used instead of the original 'much better than'. The negative form here is dictated by 'nearly', as it is only used in the negative in a structure like this one.

sentence_given: Students must attend all classes on time.
incomplete_phrase: Students ... all classes on time.
explanation: We use a straightforward active to passive voice transformation. Make sure to keep the tense consistent with the original sentence.

sentence_given: They say that success comes to those who work for it.
incomplete_phrase: There ... success comes to those who work for it.
explanation: Remember that 'belief' is the noun, whereas 'believe' is the verb form - an easy mistake to make that could ruin the transformation.

sentence_given: During my stay in Canada I met some old friends.
incomplete_phrase: I ... during my stay in Canada.
explanation: A phrasal verb 'to come across' means to meet somebody, especially if that was not planned or intentional.

sentence_given: I had to run after the bus not to miss it.
incomplete_phrase: In ... I had to run after it.
explanation: Keep in mind the five word limit in the gap - that is why 'in order not to miss the bus' is wrong - it goes over the limit.

sentence_given: After you wash the dishes you should rinse them thoroughly.
incomplete_phrase: Dishes ... after washing.
acceptable_answers: require a through rinse/require thorough rinsing
explanation: In the case of 'rinse' we need an indefinite article as the noun is in the singular. However, in the second case we refer to the activity in general, so the gerund 'rinsing' requires no indefinite article. 'Require to be rinsed' is not a correct form and shouldn't be used.

sentence_given: The building got demolished because of its poor state.
incomplete_phrase: The ... was its poor state.
explanation: Both phrases do not alter the original meaning of change, at the same time making the necessary switch to passive voice.

sentence_given: There was no connection between her mood and the weather.
incomplete_phrase: Her mood ... the weather.
explanation: A good phrase to show connection between things. Keep in mind that the tense has to be consistent with the original sentence - changing the meaning slightly, keeping the grammar and the message correct will mean you get 1 of the 2 possible points for the task.

sentence_given: Michael told me that we should talk before the meeting.
incomplete_phrase: Michael told me ... before the meeting..
explanation: To have a word means to discuss something, to have a conversation. Note that 'we need to have a word' has the same meaning, but exceeds the limit of five words dictated by the task.

sentence_given: I need somebody to fix my car before we can leave.
incomplete_phrase: I need ... before we can leave.
explanation: A structure that shows that someone else does the work for you or provides you with a service. "I need to fix my car" is incorrect as it would imply that you do the work yourself, which is clearly not the case in the original sentence.

sentence_given: Bob and I like the same movies.
incomplete_phrase: Bob has ... I do.
acceptable_answers: the same taste in movies as
explanation: The idea of "taste" here is about preferences when it comes to something - what one likes and dislikes. Using 'similar' instead of 'same' is not recommended as the first word does not mean that you like exactly the same movies, but movies that are like those.

sentence_given: I made a sandwich for you to make you feel better.
incomplete_phrase: To ... you a sandwich.
explanation: When we cheer somebody up, we try to improve their mood or try to make them feel better about themselves, especially in a bad situation or circumstances.

sentence_given: We won despite the fact the other team was much stronger.
incomplete_phrase: They ... was much weaker.
explanation: "They" in the transformed sentence clearly points to the other team. "Even though" is a contrasting structure similar to "in spite of" and "despite".

sentence_given: I didn't expect her to win the competition.
incomplete_phrase: Her victory ... as a surprise to me.
explanation: One part of "come as a surprise" is already given in the second half of the transformed sentence, so the rest shouldn't be difficult if you are familiar with the phrase.

sentence_given: I can't see why we shouldn't trust Richard's judgment.
incomplete_phrase: There ... not to trust Richard's judgment.
explanation: Make sure to add "for us" as it is a part of the original sentence, otherwise you will likely lose one of the two points for this sentence.

sentence_given: I wish I went to your party
incomplete_phrase: I ... to your party.
explanation: Verb pattern of regret requires an -ing form of the verb that follows. Giving the answer 'not attending your party' is not recommended as it introduces a more formal language structure. This would normally give you only 1 of the 2 possible points.

sentence_given: "How much money do they pay you" Michael asked me.
incomplete_phrase: Michael ... they paid me.
explanation: Present Simple to Past Simple transformation in the reported speech is already done for you here - in the key word. Do not be tempted to include 'money' at the end, as it would break the word limit of 5 words in the answer.

sentence_given: She doesn't usually come so early.
incomplete_phrase: It ... come so early.
explanation: Getting the right preposition is probably the only difficult part here. 'Uncommon with' is incorrect.

sentence_given: Teachers see Johan as the brightest student in the class.
incomplete_phrase: Among teachers, Johan ... the brightest student in the class.
acceptable_answers: Is considered as/is considered to be
explanation: Note that 'to consider as' is a much less used variant, but it is still acceptable.

sentence_given: The current policy is very likely to change.
incomplete_phrase: There are ... the current policy will change.
explanation: The phrase 'All the chances' is less known, but it fits the context just as well as the more common 'high chances'. Note the definite article in 'all the chances' - it is an integral part of this set phrase and should not be removed.

sentence_given: I can't wait for the summer break.
incomplete_phrase: I ... the summer break.
explanation: If you look forward to something, it means you want it to happen as soon as possible because of how interesting, attractive or enjoyable it is going to be.

sentence_given: When I was younger, I used to spend more time outdoors.
incomplete_phrase: I ... when I was younger.
explanation: Both "would" and "used to" are ways of expressing something that happened in the past, but does not happen now. Remember that "would" is only used for past actions, whereas "used to" is both for past actions as well as past states.

sentence_given: She has no plans to join the competition this year.
incomplete_phrase: She ... competition this year.
explanation: Answering 'will not be participating in the' is incorrect for the reason of the 5-word limit.

sentence_given: I support the idea that we join forces in this situation.
incomplete_phrase: I ... forces in this situation.
explanation: To be in favour of doing something; the -ing form is dictated by the phrase 'to be in favour' here.

sentence_given: You don't have to do your homework today.
incomplete_phrase: There ... your homework today.
explanation: It is not necessary to do it. The trick is to understand you can't just replace 'have' with 'need' and call it a day - naturally, more transformation is needed here.

sentence_given: Sarah is not going to help you with this matter.
incomplete_phrase: Sarah ... you with this matter.
explanation: The negative form is formed with the help of adding 'no' to the sentence. Note that the phrase requires the usage of the -ing form of 'helping'.

sentence_given: Many colleagues have a lot of respect for him because of his professionalism.
incomplete_phrase: Many colleagues ... because of his professionalism.
explanation: A phrasal verb that means that somebody respects somebody or holds them in high regard.

sentence_given: I am just browsing your wares right now.
incomplete_phrase: I am just ... your wares right now.
explanation: The original sentence might be a bit confusing - to browse means to look through something, such as things at a shop. The word 'internet browser' should give you an idea of other usages for it. Both 'take a look' and 'have a look' fit well here.

sentence_given: "Get a driving licence as soon as you can" my father told me.
incomplete_phrase: My father ... a driving licence.
explanation: The word 'urge' already implies that something has to be done as soon as possible, that is why the original phrasing can be made shorter.

sentence_given: Linda criticised me for failing the exam.
incomplete_phrase: Linda ... for failing the exam.
explanation: To tell somebody off means to reprimand or criticise somebody for doing something. Good knowledge of phrasal verbs is essential to getting a high score in Part 4 of FCE Use of English.

sentence_given: You should know all the exits in case there is a fire.
incomplete_phrase: You should know all the exits ... a fire.
explanation: If (or when) something happens or takes place.

sentence_given: I wasn't planning to go on a package tour for our vacation.
incomplete_phrase: Package tour was not ... for our vacation.
explanation: Here, 'to have something in mind' means to have some plan or opinion regarding something. Don't forget that Past Simple is needed to maintain tense consistency with the original sentence.

sentence_given: You have to clean these shoes well before you can wear them.
incomplete_phrase: These shoes are ... before you can wear them.
explanation: The option of 'thorough' is included as an answer because 'thorough cleaning' is a well-established collocation.

sentence_given: I used to cycle much more often when I was younger.
incomplete_phrase: I don't ... I did when I was younger.
explanation: We introduce a comparative structure to draw parallels between what happens now and how it was in the past.

sentence_given: Meteorologists say that the weather is going to improve.
incomplete_phrase: The weather ... according to meteorologists.
explanation: A simple active-to-passive voice transformation that is quite common for FCE Use of English Part 4.

sentence_given: I am going to pass the exams as long as I study hard for them.
incomplete_phrase: I am going to pass the exams ... for them.
explanation: The phrase 'provided that' is basically a fancy replacement for 'if' - in other words, a way to introduce a conditional sentence. 'That' is optional and can be omitted here.

sentence_given: We received a hateful letter as an answer to our policy.
incomplete_phrase: The ... to our policy was a hateful letter.
explanation: The difficulty here might be understanding whether 'response' should be a noun or a verb. Stay focused spell 'received' correctly - it is one of the most often misspelled words. 'That we' should be added to keep the original meaning intact, even though grammatically it is not necessary.

sentence_given: Angela asked us to talk about something else.
incomplete_phrase: Angela wanted to ... to a different one.
explanation: To change the topic of conversation, to talk about something else.

sentence_given: Richard said that it would be great if we came to meet him at the airport.
incomplete_phrase: Richard said he ... came to meet him at the airport.
explanation: An unusual transformation where we let go of the adjective and use a verb to convey a similar idea. 'It' is optional, given the 5 word limit.

sentence_given: This is the tool he invented before leaving the country.
incomplete_phrase: This tool is ... before leaving the country.
explanation: A phrasal verb 'to come up with something' that means 'to invent, to create something original'. One wrong answer is 'what came to his mind' - it fits the word limit, but it doesn't say whether he actually created it, he could have just thought about it.

sentence_given: I can't understand his ideas at all.
incomplete_phrase: His ideas ... at all.
explanation: If something makes no (or little) sense to you, it means you don't understand it or have difficulty understanding it. Note that if we used 'little' it would alter the meaning slightly, taking one of the two possible points for this task.

sentence_given: In addition to your poor academic record you keep skipping classes.
incomplete_phrase: You keep skipping classes, ... poor academic record.
explanation: A structure that can be used to introduce some additional idea, especially one that is negative and reinforces the negative aspect of the situation.

sentence_given: I could really use an hour of sleep now.
incomplete_phrase: I could ... an hour of sleep now.
explanation: If you could do with something, it means you want or need it very much. 'Really' has to be included to maintain the original meaning and get both points for the task.

sentence_given: I tend to trust people of his social status.
incomplete_phrase: I ... people of his social status.
explanation: A very simple synonymisation. If you are inclined to do something, it means you have a tendency to do it.

sentence_given: You can spend the night here if you promise to keep it down.
incomplete_phrase: You can spend the night here ... keep it down.
explanation: Another structure commonly used in this part of FCE Use of English, 'on condition that' does exactly what it says - introduces a condition, e.g. "You will get the money on condition that you promise to spend it wisely".

sentence_given: Julia asked me to help her renovate the apartment.
incomplete_phrase: Julia asked me to ... renovating the apartment.
explanation: While 'to offer a hand' is a well-known phrase, using it in this context doesn't make sense as you cannot ask somebody to offer you something.

sentence_given: I don't think you should take part in that risky venture.
incomplete_phrase: If ... not take part in that risky venture.
explanation: Here, we are looking a structure of an imaginary, unreal situation. The plural 'were' is often used to convey this idea, e.g. 'If we were to decide, we would make/would have made a better choice'.

sentence_given: Our senior manager appointed me to this position.
incomplete_phrase: I was ... our senior manager.
explanation: A regular active-to-passive voice transformation. Be aware that 'appoint as' is used in a context where the title or the position is stated explicitly, e.g. 'Judy was appointed as the head of our department'.

sentence_given: I expected Helen to marry John.
incomplete_phrase: Helen's decision to marry John ... to me.
acceptable_answers: Was not a surprise/Came as no surprise
explanation: Answering 'Did not surprise' is incorrect as the last part of the sentence goes 'to me', so you are forced to use the keyword as a noun, not as a verb.

sentence_given: "Don't spend too much money on fast food" my mother said.
incomplete_phrase: My mother ... spending too much money on fast food.
acceptable_answers: Advised me against/Advised me to avoid
explanation: Both options work well with the -ing form of 'spend' that comes right after the gap. 'To advise against' means to suggest that somebody shouldn't be doing something. Make sure to spell 'advise' correctly, as a very similar word 'advice' is a noun, whereas we are looking for a verb here.

sentence_given: How much time do you need to get to our place?
incomplete_phrase: How long ... to get to our place?.
explanation: The phrase 'take you' refers to how much time somebody needs for something, e.g. 'it didn't take me long to realise I wasn't invited to the party'.

sentence_given: You should fix your bicycle before going on this long trip.
incomplete_phrase: You ... your bicycle before going on this long trip.
explanation: Note that this is not a case of Past Perfect tense, even though it might look like one. Keeping this in mind, we do not need to put the verb in the Past Participle form.

sentence_given: I am still struggling with the new accounting system.
incomplete_phrase: I still ... the new accounting system.
acceptable_answers: Did not get/Have not got used to
explanation: While 'still' normally accompanies a Present Perfect form ('still haven't got'), it is acceptable to use Past Simple here ('still did not get') as the original sentence does not explicitly limit us in the choice of tense. Note that 'I still am not used...' is incorrect as 'still' should be put after the auxiliary 'am'.

sentence_given: Why do you still have that old TV?
incomplete_phrase: Why haven't ... that old TV yet?
explanation: Contrary to the previous sentence, our choice in this one is dictated by 'have' just before the gap. It forces us to stick to the Present Perfect form.

sentence_given: George has an annoying habit of taking things that do not belong to him.
incomplete_phrase: George ... things that do not belong to him.
explanation: The biggest difficulty here is to understand that we have to use Present Continuous to express how annoyed we are with his habit. As a general rule, the structure 'always + -ing verb' is used to show that we dislike somebody's repeated action or manner of doing something.

sentence_given: 'Do your friends like this place?' asked the landlord.
incomplete_phrase: The landlord ... liked that place.
correct_answer: wanted to know if my friends
acceptable_answers: wanted to know if my friends
explanation: Reported speech with a yes/no question (a question that can only receive 'yes' or 'no' as the answer). We introduce it with an 'if' structure. 'Wanted to ask' is incorrect, as the landlord clearly asked, not simply wanted to do so.

sentence_given: We are pretty similar in our food preferences.
incomplete_phrase: There isn't ... food preferences.
explanation: We are forced to use the opposite word (similarity-difference) because of the negative structure in the first part of the sentence. 'Difference between' and 'difference in' in this context are interchangeable, however, in certain context they can have different meaning. 'Difference in' refers to a particular aspect where things are not the same, whereas 'difference between' talks about a general dissimilarity.

sentence_given: We have almost no money left
incomplete_phrase: We have almost ... money.
explanation: A phrasal verbs which means that something such as money, patience or any other thing has ended or come to an end. Note the forms of the irregular verb 'to run' goes RUN-RAN-RUN.

sentence_given: The jury asked me to describe what happened that night.
incomplete_phrase: I was ... to describe what happened that night.
explanation: We use a passive voice form and mention the agent (the jury), introducing it with 'by'.

sentence_given: To everyone's surprise, their new album was a great hit.
incomplete_phrase: Nobody ... become a great hit.
explanation: A paraphrased structure with some leeway in word choice at the end. Very often, the context in the second sentence forces you to approach the task with a paraphrase or a negative form.

sentence_given: The coach thinks he is not ready for the competition.
incomplete_phrase: The coach ... is ready for the competition.
explanation: The word 'feel' is used in the meaning 'have an opinion, believe'. 'That' is optional - note that sometimes the optional 'that' might exceed the word limit of 5 words. In a case like that, it obviously has to be omitted.

sentence_given: George promised he would handle the situation.
incomplete_phrase: George ... he would handle the situation.
explanation: To give your word means to promise something. Another case with an omittable 'that'.

sentence_given: It took Jane two years to forget her boyfriend.
incomplete_phrase: It took Jane two years ... her boyfriend.
explanation: If you get over something, it means that you cope with or forget some unpleasant memory such as loss, breaking up and so on.

sentence_given: Do you want to go dancing or to the movies?
incomplete_phrase: Would ... dancing or to the movies?
explanation: A 'would rather' structure, used to indicate one's preference or choice between several options. If you would rather do it, it means you want to do it more than something else.

sentence_given: The crime was prevented because the police arrived early enough.
incomplete_phrase: The police ... the crime.
explanation: Note the difference between 'in time' and 'on time'. 'In time' means soon enough, before it was too late. 'On time' means at some particular moment in time that was agreed upon, e.g. 'to arrive to the meeting on time' as opposed to 'to arrive in time to catch the last bus'.

sentence_given: The celebration will be held inside the building of a local museum.
incomplete_phrase: The celebration ... inside the building of a local museum.
explanation: Both options stick to the general meaning of the original sentence. Note that 'will be taking' is a more formal way to convey the idea, and it emphasises the fact that the event has been planned in advance.

sentence_given: The rival team lost to us in the final round.
incomplete_phrase: We ... in the final round.
explanation: 'Beat' is an irregular verb that has both the first and second forms identical - the main challenge of this transformation.

sentence_given: The car was so expensive that we ended up not buying it.
incomplete_phrase: The price of ... that we ended up not buying it.
explanation: We are looking for 'of the' structure here, as dictated by the first part of the transformed sentence. Be mindful not to answer 'was too high' as we are looking for a comparative structure to stick to the original meaning.

sentence_given: Judy always finds it easy to talk to people she doesn't know well.
incomplete_phrase: Judy never ... to people she doesn't know well.
explanation: Do not use a double negative structure, e.g. 'Never has no difficulty' as grammatically it is incorrect, even though you can see it used in movies as a dialect.

sentence_given: The housemaid is going to vacuum the flat while we are out.
incomplete_phrase: We are going to ... the housemaid while we are out.
explanation: The structure highlights the fact that somebody else is carrying out the action - the housemaid in this case.

sentence_given: There aren't many similarities between me and Josh.
incomplete_phrase: Josh has ... with me.
acceptable_answers: Very little / Almost nothing in common
explanation: A phrase 'to have in common' fits the idea of showing similarities (or lack of said similarities) between somebody or something.

sentence_given: I doubt Michael is brave enough to join the navy.
incomplete_phrase: I believe ... to join the navy.
explanation: Answering 'Michael does not have the bravery' is grammatically acceptable, but it exceeds the imposed word limit. This limitation is often forgotten by the test-takers, so keep that factor in mind.

sentence_given: Nobody mentioned the problem during the meeting.
incomplete_phrase: During the meeting ... the problem.
explanation: If you bring something up, you mention or discuss it. Be ready to see at least a couple phrasal verb transformation in your FCE Use of English Part 4 exam task.

sentence_given: "Come to my place for dinner tonight" he said.
incomplete_phrase: He invited us ... dinner tonight.
explanation: To visit, especially for a particular occasion such as a meal or a celebration. Pay attention to the fact that despite using reported speech, we do not make the switch to the past tense - using 'invited' is enough in this case.

sentence_given: We had almost no chances of catching the train.
incomplete_phrase: We ... of catching the train.
explanation: The adverb 'hardly' introduces the negative aspect needed in the transformation, so 'any' has to included as well.

sentence_given: I have last seen Simon a long time ago.
incomplete_phrase: It ... since I last saw Simon.
explanation: A set phrase with the meaning that a lot of time has passed since some event. Make sure to use Present Perfect, otherwise you might lose 1 point for introducing an unnecessary change in the meaning.

sentence_given: Nothing prevents us from going on a trip right now.
incomplete_phrase: Nothing ... us going on a trip right now.
explanation: Another phrase, this time it means that something acts as an obstacle. Note that 'nothing' is singular, so the verb has to be in the singular form as well.

sentence_given: Kevin doesn't speak the local language too well.
incomplete_phrase: Kevin's ... is not too good.
explanation: As a learner and an exam-taker of FCE, you should be well familiar with 'command of language'. It means how skilled you are in a language.

sentence_given: Even though we were late to the party, we didn't miss much.
incomplete_phrase: In ... to the party, we didn't miss much.
explanation: A structure to introduce contrast in the sentence with some freedom of choice.

sentence_given: I train so much but I still feel anxious before every competition.
incomplete_phrase: No ... I still fell anxious before every competition.
explanation: If something doesn't matter, then it makes no difference, it has no significant effect. It can also mean that it is not important (but not in the context of this sentence).

sentence_given: They promised to pay us on time.
incomplete_phrase: We ... on time.
explanation: We are switching from active voice in the original sentence to passive voice - a common transformation in FCE Use of English Part 4.

sentence_given: The only thing I want is to try this.
incomplete_phrase: To have ... this is all I want.
explanation: If you have a go at something, you try to do it, you make an attempt to do it. Interestingly, 'to have a go at someone' means to blame or critisize them.

sentence_given: "Call me when you get home" said Melinda.
incomplete_phrase: Melinda asked me ... I got home.
explanation: A simple paraphrase here - if you do something the moment something happens, you do it immediately after that. Also note the required transformations when you convert direct speech to indirect.

sentence_given: Even though my salary is higher, I still have financial difficulties.
incomplete_phrase: The ... didn't help with my financial difficulties.
explanation: The definite article in the beginning forces us to use 'increase' as a noun, rather than a verb. In this case, 'my' is optional, as the context clearly points at whose salary we are talking about. Moreover, we already have one 'my' in the second part of the paraphrased sentence.

sentence_given: I was about to leave when the phone rang.
incomplete_phrase: The phone rang when I was ... leaving.
explanation: To be on/at the point of doing something means to be about to or ready to do it. It is normally used in cases where the person chooses not to take the intended action.

sentence_given: When you drive fast, you endanger other motorists.
incomplete_phrase: You ... when you drive fast.
explanation: If you put somebody at risk, you expose them to danger. Even though grammatically you can answer "You are putting other motorists at risk", remember that your answer should not exceed 5 words.

sentence_given: We went to the same college and that's why we became good friends.
incomplete_phrase: I wouldn't have become good friends with him ... to the same college.
explanation: A case of Third Conditional sentence is present here. Be ready to see (and know how to use) all types of mixed conditionals in FCE Use of English Part 4.

sentence_given: "I can lend you some money if you like" Josh said.
incomplete_phrase: Josh ... some money.
explanation: Be careful not to confuse the words 'lend' and 'borrow'. To borrow is to take money from somebody in order to pay it back later, whereas to lend is to give the money and receive it later.

sentence_given: My shyness makes it difficult for me to meet new people.
incomplete_phrase: My shyness ... new people easily.
explanation: The structure 'Prevents from' requires a gerund form.

sentence_given: I didn't expect him to know math so well.
incomplete_phrase: His ... a surprise to me.
explanation: Try to stay as close to the original as possible - so turning 'know' into 'knowledge' is the only viable option. This is also important for tense consistency - both the original and the changed sentences are in Past Simple.

sentence_given: I offered him 100 dollars for the book.
incomplete_phrase: I ... 100 dollars for the book.
explanation: Do not be tempted to use verbs in the past, e.g. "I decided to offer him" - first of all, you won't be able to squeeze them into the 5 word limit, and secondly, the meaning of the original sentence will be changed as a result. Another key thing is when you introduce a number in a word like 'offer' or 'amount', it should come with the 'of' preposition.

sentence_given: The kids should really go to bed now.
incomplete_phrase: It's ... to bed now.
explanation: The expression 'It's high time somebody did something' means that the time for it has come or is past due. Note that the phrase 'It is high time' is normally followed by a structure in the Past Simple.

sentence_given: The fireworks could be heard exploding from a mile away.
incomplete_phrase: I could hear ... from a mile away..
explanation: The phrasal verb 'to go off' in this context means to explore or to make a distinct noise. Answering 'The fireworks were going to explode' would obviously be wrong, as the action has already taken place according to the original sentence.

sentence_given: Mary managed to convince me not to quit the job.
incomplete_phrase: Mary managed to ... the job.
explanation: If you change somebody's mind it means you convince them to change their decision or opinion regarding something.

sentence_given: I found it difficult to reach the train station.
incomplete_phrase: I had ... the train station.
explanation: To have difficulties doing something should be pretty self-explanatory - it means that something wasn't easy for somebody.

sentence_given: Because I wanted to get scholarship at university, I had to study hard.
incomplete_phrase: I had to study hard ... scholarship at university.
acceptable_answers: As I wanted to get/So as to get
explanation: A rather straightforward structure to show the reason for some particular action. The second suggested structure is more advanced and is more commonly used by C1/C2 speakers.

sentence_given: I refused their promotion offer for personal reasons.
incomplete_phrase: For personal reasons, ... down.
explanation: If you turn something down, you reject or decline it. It can be used for figurative cases (e.g. an offer) or literal (a gift or other material thing).

sentence_given: Mother told me to finish eating all the potatoes before I could get dessert.
incomplete_phrase: Mother told me to ... before I could get dessert.
acceptable_answers: Eat up the potatoes/Eat the potatoes up
explanation: To eat something up in this context has the meaning to eat all of it, to finish eating a dish or a meal. Do not use 'finish up' as it is not normally used in relation to food.

sentence_given: We occasionally meet at this pub.
incomplete_phrase: We meet at this pub ... time.
explanation: If something takes place from time to time, then it happens fairly regularly, but without any definite system or timetable.

sentence_given: I used to go to the cinema every Tuesday when I was in college.
incomplete_phrase: When I was in college I ... every Tuesday.
explanation: The original sentence expresses the idea that the speaker no longer does that. A structure that is quite similar to 'used to', it is only used with actions, while 'used to' can be used both with actions and states.

sentence_given: My camera broke down on my first day of vacation.
incomplete_phrase: My camera ... on my first day of vacation.
explanation: Please note that 'break apart' is incorrect in this context as it means 'to disassemble, to take apart', whereas we are looking for a phrasal verb that means 'to stop functioning'.

sentence_given: I wanted to see the sea this summer
incomplete_phrase: I ... the sea this summer.
explanation: Be careful not to answer "Was going to the sea" - it means a more definite plan that involves somebody else. Remember that we use Present Continuous to express a more definite plan that takes others into account.

sentence_given: Grandmother often asks me to read the newspaper aloud for her.
incomplete_phrase: Grandmother often asks me to ... for her.
acceptable_answers: Read out the newspaper/Read the newspaper out/Read the newspaper out loud
explanation: To read something out means to read it aloud for somebody to hear. 'To read out loud' is also possible and is probably the first choice for most students at this level.

sentence_given: "You may enter the room" said Mary.
incomplete_phrase: Mary ... the room.
explanation: Both the original and the changed sentence should use a structure that gives permission to do something.

sentence_given: It took me a year to wake up easily in the morning.
incomplete_phrase: It took me a year to ... easily in the morning.
explanation: We use the structure 'to get used to doing something' to express the idea of making a new habit, especially something that previously was not a part of our routine. Note the gerund form that is required in this structure.

sentence_given: We have never had such an exciting trip before.
incomplete_phrase: This is the most ... had.
explanation: The switch from 'never' to 'ever' requires some additional changes in the transformed sentence. Make sure to keep the changed sentence in the Present Perfect.

sentence_given: In the end, we changed our decision about buying the boat.
incomplete_phrase: In the end, we ... the boat.
explanation: To decide against doing something is to choose not to do it. Note the -ing form that is used with this structure. The sentence 'We changed our decision against buying the boat' has double a negative meaning, which means that the speaker chose to buy it, which is not the message of the original sentence.

sentence_given: Can you still draw well?
incomplete_phrase: Are ... draw well?
explanation: The beginning of the sentence forces us to look for an adjective instead of the verb in the original sentence. Failing to include 'still' will make you lose 1 of the 2 points for this sentence.

sentence_given: All I wanted was to escape this place.
incomplete_phrase: All I wanted was to ... this place.
explanation: Both of the phrasal verbs mean 'to leave some place'. Be careful to use the appropriate participle with each phrasal verb.

sentence_given: There was plenty of food for everyone at the party.
incomplete_phrase: There was ... for everyone at the party.
explanation: The phrase 'plenty of' means that there is no shortage of something, that it is available in great numbers or quantity.

sentence_given: "Have you ever though about retiring?" asked Suze.
incomplete_phrase: Suze wanted to know if ... retirement.
explanation: Remember to make the necessary transformation associated with reported speech. Here, Present Perfect to Past perfect change is optional as the idea works in both tenses. Remember than sometimes the tense change in reported speech is not necessary, particularly in cases with past experiences plans that affect the present situation.

sentence_given: I expected more from the meeting.
incomplete_phrase: I ... the meeting.
explanation: If you are underwhelmed by something, it means that it was less impressive or interesting than you had expected. Be careful not to answer 'got underwhelmed by'.

sentence_given: I have never been to this city before.
incomplete_phrase: This is ... this city.
explanation: While the phrase 'my first time' is easy to get, pay attention to the preposition that follows the phrase.

sentence_given: She decided to donate most of the money to various charities.
incomplete_phrase: She ... the money to various charities.
explanation: To give something away means to give it to somebody without asking or expecting anything in return.

sentence_given: Richard is much less experienced than Dan.
incomplete_phrase: Dan ... experience than Richard.
explanation: 'Far' is used as an intensifier, similarly to 'much' in the first sentence. Don't be misguided by the inverted word order in the transformed sentence.

sentence_given: "I am sorry I interrupted your conversation" Giorgio said.
incomplete_phrase: Giorgio ... conversation.
explanation: Both spelling variants of the word 'to apologise' are acceptable. Make sure to change 'your conversation' to 'our conversation'. Saying 'my conversation' makes no logical sense as it means that only one person was involved in it.

sentence_given: Please keep in mind that you will be charged for the service as well as the food.
incomplete_phrase: Please ... you will be charged for the service as well as the food.
explanation: The expression 'be advised' is mostly found in formal texts such as notices, and they usually warn you about something important. 'Advice' is spelling for the noun, whereas 'advise' is the verb that we are looking for.

sentence_given: I never realised that they were twins.
incomplete_phrase: It ... they were twins.
explanation: If something occurs to you, it means that it crosses your mind, you think about it. The opposite structure is used here.

sentence_given: They had to cancel the meeting because some senior managers couldn't make there in time.
incomplete_phrase: The meeting had ... because some senior managers couldn't make there in time.
explanation: To call something off means to cancel a previously planned arrangement, especially one that involved preparation and many people were supposed to be a part of it.

sentence_given: The elevator didn't work so we had to use the stairs to get to the seventh floor.
incomplete_phrase: The elevator ... so we had to use the stairs to get to the seventh floor.
explanation: 'Out of order' is normally used with larger machinery that does not function properly. It is often written on signs that warn those who plan to use it that it is currently unavailable. A good example is public elevators.

sentence_given: Even though Rob tried his best, he came second in the race.
incomplete_phrase: Rob came second in the race ... his best.
explanation: A common situation is when students confuse 'in spite of' and 'despite'. We need the first, longer structure.

sentence_given: I will help you with the project if you promise to study harder next year.
incomplete_phrase: I will help you with the project ... you promise to study harder next year.
explanation: The definite article in the second variant is optional, as both ways of phrasing are quite common.

sentence_given: "Be careful, there is a storm coming from the sea" said the old lady.
incomplete_phrase: The old lady ... a storm coming from the sea.
explanation: An interesting thing about this one is that technically you can use 'told us about' as the answer. However, this would fail to include the part where she stresses the danger of the situation. 'To warn about something' is the perfect phrase for that.

sentence_given: He drew my attention to my most serious mistakes.
incomplete_phrase: He ... most serious mistakes.
explanation: Note that with 'point out' you do not need a preposition 'to' from the original sentence.

sentence_given: You always leave the most difficult tasks until later.
incomplete_phrase: You always ... most difficult tasks.
explanation: Putting something off means leaving it for later - that's why the transformed sentence omits the last part of the original one ('until later').

sentence_given: We spend four days moving all the furniture into the new flat.
incomplete_phrase: It ... move all the furniture into the new flat.
explanation: A phrase to show that you need a certain amount of time for a particular action. Don't forget to make the switch to Past Simple!

sentence_given: Liam was too slow and missed the morning train.
incomplete_phrase: Liam ... catch the morning train.
explanation: Answering 'did not have enough time' is incorrect for two reasons. First, we need 'to' and there is no way to squeeze it into the given word limit without sacrificing meaning. Second, it is not about shortage of time, but about Liam being slow.

sentence_given: My mother was the only one to come to the party.
incomplete_phrase: Nobody came ... my mother.
explanation: Be careful not to answer 'except FROM', as the correct phrasing is 'except FOR'.

sentence_given: "Don't come close to me" the stranger told me.
incomplete_phrase: The stranger ... to him.
explanation: Both verbs work well with the preposition 'against' to show that somebody tells you it is not a good idea to do something. Note that the gerund form should follow both structures. Be mindful of the spelling: 'advise' is the verb and 'advice' is the noun spelling variant.

sentence_given: She said that she succeeded because of sheer luck.
incomplete_phrase: She ... sheer luck.
acceptable_answers: Put her success down to/Put down her success to
explanation: To put something down to something else means to give something as a reason. In this case, her determination was the reason for her success.

sentence_given: "Do you have any questions?" asked Jan.
incomplete_phrase: Jan wanted ... any questions.
explanation: Even though 'whether' is a perfect replacement for 'if', you should not be using it because 'if' is given as a key word here and has to be present in the sentence.

sentence_given: We don't know for sure if they have met before.
incomplete_phrase: It ... they have met before.
explanation: If you can't tell something, it means that you have no information about it or you can't be sure about the things you know. Note the interchangeability of 'if' and 'whether'.

sentence_given: His family hasn't heard the news yet.
incomplete_phrase: His family ... the news.
correct_answer: still has not read the news
acceptable_answers: still has not read the news
Still have/has not read the news
still have not read the news
explanation: The word 'family' grammatically can be both singular and plural, depending on whether we mean the family as a whole or each person individually.

sentence_given: When do you expect Charles to return?
incomplete_phrase: When ... back?
explanation: Apart from using a phrasal verb, we resort to the Present Continuous to underline the fact of a planned event.

sentence_given: He began studying two months ago.
incomplete_phrase: He ... two months.
explanation: We cannot avoid using Present Perfect Continuous - we need the Perfect part because we are not using 'two months ago', but simply 'two months'. The Continuous part is dictated by the preposition 'for'.

sentence_given: Bob and Marie seem to have a good relationship.
incomplete_phrase: Bob and Marie ... with one another.
explanation: To get along means to be in good or friendly relationship with somebody.

sentence_given: "I will need you both to help me with this" said Sandra.
incomplete_phrase: Sandra said that she ... to help her with that.
acceptable_answers: Would require both of us/us both
explanation: Changing 'will' to 'would' in reported speech is a common thing that is done almost always, unlike switching to a different tense, which is more context-sensitive.

sentence_given: They told us not to buy that plot of land.
incomplete_phrase: We ... buying that plot of land.
explanation: Because the second part of the sentence starts with 'buying' we have to use a structure that works well with a gerund form. The second answer is much less likely to be given by a B2 learner, but it is included just in case.

sentence_given: Children nowadays prefer superhero movies to cartoons.
incomplete_phrase: Children nowadays ... than cartoons.
explanation: Using 'would' helps us create an imaginary situation where the children are given a choice of things to see (or to watch!).

sentence_given: The weather was much better than predicted.
incomplete_phrase: The weather ... as predicted.
explanation: 'As' that comes right after the gap hints at a comparative structure that uses two of these words. The word 'nearly' is optional and does not grant you any additional points.

sentence_given: Matt should consider improving his command of English.
incomplete_phrase: Matt should consider ... command of English.
explanation: If you brush up on something, you make it slightly better. Used figuratively to talk about skills and areas of knowledge.

sentence_given: The train should arrive any minute now.
incomplete_phrase: The train ... any minute now.
explanation: It might take a bit of figuring out to understand that 'to' forces us to stick to passive voice in this sentence.

sentence_given: "You had to hand in this paper two days ago" said the professor.
incomplete_phrase: The professor said I had to hand in ... yesterday.
explanation: Giving a simpler answer like 'hand in that paper before yesterday' would only give you one point, as the idea is to see your paraphrasing and transformation skills required for reported speech usage. Don't forget about 'this' to 'that' transofrmation.

sentence_given: Our teacher promised to take us on a field trip next summer.
incomplete_phrase: Our teacher ... take us on a field trip next summer.
explanation: A set phrase, 'to give (your) word' means to promise something. Note that because 'promised' is in the past, we should be using 'would' instead of 'will' from the original sentence to maintain tense consistency.

sentence_given: Stefani came to deal with the computer problem I'm having.
incomplete_phrase: Stefani came to ... I'm having.
explanation: To sort something out is to figure out or overcome some problem, issue, or difficulty. Interestingly, you could answer 'to HELP OUT WITH the computer problem' if it weren't for the word limit.

sentence_given: We didn't expect you to arrive so early.
incomplete_phrase: We didn't ... so early.
explanation: Note the structure "count on somebody doing something". The -ing form is needed here. Otherwise, you can stick to the infinitive form.

sentence_given: I can't get to work on time without my car.
incomplete_phrase: I ... to get to work on time.
explanation: If you rely on something, you can't do without it.

sentence_given: Nancy was sure that you would come to the party.
incomplete_phrase: Nancy ... would come to the party.
explanation: A possible answer is 'had no doubts about you coming'. Naturally, we cannot use it here because we are only allowed to change the words within the gap.

sentence_given: The shop gave me a discount as a compensation for the inconvenience.
incomplete_phrase: The shop gave me a discount ... the inconvenience.
explanation: To make up for something means to compensate for a loss, to try and fix a mistake, to right a wrong. It can be used in relation to both people and inanimate objects.

sentence_given: "You will miss your flight if you don't hurry" my brother said.
incomplete_phrase: My brother said that ... miss my flight.
explanation: We are making a reported speech structure with all the usual changes. 'Unless' usually has a meaning similar to 'if not', in this case 'if I didn't'.

sentence_given: They plan to renovate the city centre next year.
incomplete_phrase: The city centre ... next year.
acceptable_answers: Is due to be renovated/due for a renovation
explanation: When something is due, it means that there is a plan to do this, e.g. 'The restaurant is due to be opened tomorrow'.

sentence_given: "Did you see the memo from yesterday?" my boss asked me.
incomplete_phrase: My boss asked ... the memo from the day before.
explanation: Another reported speech case with a change from Past Simple ('… did I see') to Past Perfect ('… if I had seen'). 'The day before' in the changed sentence might seem a bit confusing, but it is in fact reminding us about the alterations that need to be made in the reported sentence structure.

sentence_given: We all have a lot of respect for our coach.
incomplete_phrase: We all ... our coach.
explanation: To look up to somebody means to have a lot of respect for them. Naturally, this phrase is only used in relation to a person.

sentence_given: As soon as I received the message I replied to it.
incomplete_phrase: I replied ... I received it.
explanation: If you do something the moment something else happens, you do it immediately after. Be careful not to omit the first 'to' here, as suggested by the original sentence. Failing to do so means losing two points for this task.

sentence_given: There is almost no time to finish the essay.
incomplete_phrase: There is ... left to finish the essay.
explanation: There is almost no time = there is hardly any time. Be prepared to paraphrase ideas in Part 4 of Use of English.

sentence_given: I am sorry I didn't see your performance live.
incomplete_phrase: I ... your performance live.
explanation: The verb pattern of 'regret' requires a gerund (an -ing form). If you regret something it means you are sorry you have made some choice in the past and are not happy with the consequences.

sentence_given: The meeting was much better than we had expected.
incomplete_phrase: The meetings was ... we had expected.
explanation: The keyword forces us to use a comparative 'as … as' structure, there is no way around it. Note that the negative form is required here.

sentence_given: Jim really disappointed his parents with the exam results.
incomplete_phrase: Jim really ... with the exam results.
explanation: If you let somebody down, you fail to meet their expectations or make them feel disappointed for some other reason.

sentence_given: We still haven't found a solution to this problem.
incomplete_phrase: We ... a solution to this problem.
explanation: 'Yet to do something' means that you haven't done it yet, but you are planning on doing it. We cannot simply put "yet" at the end of the sentence - it would work grammatically, but in FCE Use of English Part 4 we are only allowed to make changes in the designated gap.

sentence_given: I have never seen such a beautiful sunset.
incomplete_phrase: This is the ... such a beautiful sunset.
explanation: Be careful not to answer 'First time ever I am seeing' - while the meaning remains the same, you are breaking the five word limit for the answer - a common pitfall that many students tend to forget about.

sentence_given: "Please mind your step" said the gatekeeper.
incomplete_phrase: I was ... by the gatekeeper.
explanation: The keyword here is a hint for a regular infinitive form of the phrase. You get some freedom of choice with the verb here. Be careful to spell "correctly". Remember that 'advise' is the verb, whereas 'advice' is the noun.

sentence_given: I needed to think of a good excuse to skip school.
incomplete_phrase: In needed to ... a good excuse to skip school.
explanation: A phrasal verb that means 'to think of something new, to invent something'.

sentence_given: In this country people take their shoes off when at home.
incomplete_phrase: People in this country ... take their shoes off when at home.
explanation: Here we talk about a cultural rule, in other words, something that people normally do. If you are expected to do something, it means that it is what people normally do.

sentence_given: Jeremy was unsure if he should take that offer.
incomplete_phrase: Jeremy ... that offer.
explanation: While 'his' is optional here, we shouldn't be using 'some doubts' as it is not part of the original sentence. While 'his' isn't either, it is a common part of the phrase, e.g. 'I have my doubts about this'.

sentence_given: Yesterday I visited a friend and also did a washing up.
incomplete_phrase: Yesterday I did a washing up ... a friend.
explanation: The structure 'in addition to' is normally accompanied by an -ing form when we talk about an action. Therefore, it goes either 'in addition to something' or 'in addition to doing something'.

sentence_given: Our family planned to visit this country next year.
incomplete_phrase: Our family ... this country next year..
explanation: To plan on doing something. Note how the preposition affects the form of the word that comes after it - a common feature of FCE Use of English Part 4.

sentence_given: One has to do this project before tomorrow.
incomplete_phrase: The project has ... before tomorrow.
explanation: The word "one" here refers to an impersonal structure where no particular agents of action are mentioned. To carry something out means to do it.

sentence_given: Lucy accidentally met her ex-boyfriend during a skiing trip.
incomplete_phrase: Lucy ... her ex-boyfriend during a skiing trip.
explanation: The meaning of this phrasal verb is to meet with somebody without meaning or planning to, randomly, for no particular reason.

sentence_given: I don't think we are going to have rain tomorrow.
incomplete_phrase: We ... rain tomorrow.
explanation: Avoid making any unnecessary alterations to the original phrasing. Answering 'Are unlikely to get' is grammatically and lexically correct, but you might get deducted one point for introducing a change to the first sentence that just wasn't needed.

sentence_given: These math problems were too difficult for me.
incomplete_phrase: I found these math problems ... with.
explanation: If you can't deal with something, it means you are unable to face a fact or solve a problem. A small lexical footnote - math problems are various calculations that are there as a form of exercise or a part of some real project.

sentence_given: The meeting had to be cancelled for a number of reasons.
incomplete_phrase: The meeting had ... for a number of reasons.
explanation: Calling something off means cancelling it. This is a more informal way to phrase the idea, which is the case for most of phrasal verbs. However, this does not mean that phrasal verbs are mostly reserved for spoken English.

sentence_given: Be careful, as there are many poisonous snakes in this part of the woods.
incomplete_phrase: Be ... poisonous snakes in this part of the woods.
explanation: To be especially careful or vigilant to notice something, to be ready to see it. A similar verb form is spelled in two words and has a different meaning, e.g. 'I looked out of the train window'.

sentence_given: That film was more boring than we had expected.
incomplete_phrase: That film was ... we had expected.
explanation: The negative particle as the keyword means that we have to switch to words with the opposite meaning. That is why we have more choice in terms of phrasing the answer.

sentence_given: If you cannot guarantee my safety, I will not join you.
incomplete_phrase: I will not join you ... my safety.
explanation: At this point you should be pretty comfortable with 'unless' structures. The biggest mistake you can make here is to spell "guarantee" incorrectly - admittedly, an easy mistake to make.

sentence_given: There won't be any phones of this model available until next week.
incomplete_phrase: Phones of this model ... until next week.
explanation: Answering 'will be in stock' is incorrect because of the word "until". It would work in a context like 'Phones of this model will be (back) in stock next week'.

sentence_given: I spend most of the time learning the guitar.
incomplete_phrase: Most of ... learning the guitar.
explanation: The key thing here is to include "my" in the changed sentence. Even though it is absent from the original one, here it is essential to show whose time we are referring to. Without it, the sentence falls apart grammatically and in terms of its meaning.

sentence_given: I have to deliver this package before the shipment leaves the shop.
incomplete_phrase: This package ... the shop before the shipment leaves.
explanation: We do a simple reorganisation of words here, with an addition of a passive voice.

sentence_given: I am not sure why I chose accounting as my career path.
incomplete_phrase: I ... why I chose accounting as my career path.
explanation: A very easy mistake to make here is to answer 'I have a question why…'. Instead, we are expected to use the word "question" as a verb. This is a common trap you will encounter in your FCE Use of English Part 4 test.

sentence_given: "Do you mind helping me with the TV?" Marcia asked.
incomplete_phrase: Marcia ... with the TV.
acceptable_answers: Wanted me to help her/Asked me to help her
explanation: Note that the verb 'wanted' requires a so-called direct object ('me') as we want to clarify to whom the request was addressed. 'Asked' however does not necessarily need an object to work in this context.

sentence_given: Our city is known for its Olympic-sized stadium.
incomplete_phrase: Olympic-sized stadium ... known for.
explanation: Here we have an example of a cleft sentence - a special way to put emphasis on a particular part of the sentence. In this case, we put stress on the fact that the city is well-known for its stadium rather than something else.

sentence_given: Rick is quicker on his bike than Jonathan.
incomplete_phrase: Jonathan is ... Rick.
explanation: Good answers that break the word limit are 'A slower cyclist compared to/with Rick'. Don't be shy to count the words before you choose the answer.

sentence_given: You don't need to change the oil in your car so often.
incomplete_phrase: There ... the oil in your car so often.
explanation: When there is no point in doing something, it means that the action in question is not needed. In this case, the meaning is that changing the oil so often is redundant.

sentence_given: Sarah did not know about her husband had an affair with the housemaid.
incomplete_phrase: Sarah was ... that her husband had an affair with the housemaid.
explanation: Remember that your answer can be as short as two words. Using additional words in this example does not give you any additional points, so both options are equal in terms of scoring.

sentence_given: The weather here is very similar to my home country.
incomplete_phrase: The weather here is ... as in my home country.
explanation: An answer you might want to give can go like, 'The weather here feels/is more like in my home country'. However, it would be incorrect as it suggests some sort of comparison. There is no other place or country we can compare it with in this context.

sentence_given: They say that sunbathing increases the risk of skin diseases.
incomplete_phrase: Sunbathing ... the risk of skin diseases.
explanation: An impersonal structure that does not highlight what person or group of individuals hold this opinion. Instead, it generalises the idea.

sentence_given: I never realized that her father owned the whole company.
incomplete_phrase: It ... that her father owned the whole company.
explanation: If something occurs to you, then it comes to your mind, you come to the realisation that it is true. Because the key word is in the present, we have to use the auxiliary 'did' in the past to make the sentence grammatically sound.

sentence_given: The management is responsible for the current crisis.
incomplete_phrase: It is ... for the current crisis.
correct_answer: is the management we should blame
acceptable_answers: is the management we should blame
is the management we must blame
Is the management we should/must blame
explanation: Answering 'Is the management that is to blame' is grammatically correct, but it exceeds the word limit of five words.

sentence_given: We were late because of the traffic.
incomplete_phrase: Our ... to the traffic.
explanation: Remember that 'due to' is a structure that is more common for negative context. Since 'to' has to be used, we can't put 'because' at the end of the answer.

sentence_given: 'Are you expecting anyone?' my mom asked me.
incomplete_phrase: My mon ... was expecting anyone.
explanation: A classic transformation to reported speech and all the necessary changes that come with it; namely, we use past simple instead of present simple and using 'if' for a yes-no question.

sentence_given: We haven't seen many sights here.
incomplete_phrase: We ... sights here.
